knowledge:
- key_parameters: data=Input dataset as a SummarizedExperiment, matrix, or data.frame ;; classes=Vector or column containing class information for the samples ;; chr.num=The number of chromosomes in each population (default 1000) ;; chr.len=The length of each chromosome, representing the desired number of features to select ;; generat=The maximum number of generations (default 500) ;; co.rate=The probability of crossover for each random couple of chromosomes (default 0.8) ;; mut.rate=The probability of mutating each chromosome base (default 0.01) ;; n.elit=The number of best chromosomes preserved from evolution (default 10) ;; type.sel=The selection algorithm, either "RW" (Roulette Wheel) or "Tournament" ;; type.co=The crossover algorithm, either "one.p" (One point) or "two.p" (Two points) ;; type.one.p.co=The quartile where one-point crossover is applied ("I.quart", "II.quart", "III.quart") ;; n.gen.conv=The maximum consecutive generations with the same maximum fitness score to trigger early stopping (default 80) ;; plots=Whether to generate plots ("yes" or "no") ;; verbose=Whether to print progress information in the console ("yes" or "no")
- alternatives: Filter Methods (e.g. Information Gain, ReliefF, Gini Index, Chi-squared test) can be used when simple univariate ranking is sufficient. Wrapper/Embedded Methods using classifiers (e.g. GA-SVM, GA-KNN, rfGA, caretGA, GA-MLHD) can be used when feature selection needs to be tightly coupled with a specific classifier's performance, though they are more prone to overfitting than GARS.
- when_to_use: Use GARS when performing feature selection on high-dimensional datasets (such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, or metabolomics data) where the number of features greatly exceeds the sample size, and you want a robust, classifier-independent subset of features for downstream classification.
- pitfalls: Setting chr.num too small limits the search space exploration, while setting it too high makes the algorithm run very slowly. Forcing a single chr.len might not yield the absolute best feature subset; users should test multiple chromosome lengths to find the optimal number of features. Using default small values of generat (e.g., 20) or chr.num (e.g., 100) for real high-dimensional datasets may not be sufficient to find the best feature set.

workflows.name: feature_selection_gars
workflows.intent: Run the genetic algorithm to select a robust subset of features from normalized high-dimensional data and visualize the results.
input: datanorm (normalized SummarizedExperiment, matrix, or data.frame of expression data)
workflows.stages: 1. Run GARS_GA to perform genetic algorithm-based feature selection ;; 2. Extract fitness scores and plot fitness evolution ;; 3. Extract populations and plot feature usage frequency ;; 4. Extract the reduced expression matrix of selected features
workflows.code:
res_GA <- GARS_GA(data=datanorm,
                 classes = colData(datanorm),
                 chr.num = 100,
                 chr.len = 8,
                 generat = 20,
                 co.rate = 0.8,
                 mut.rate = 0.1,
                 n.elit = 10,
                 type.sel = "RW",
                 type.co = "one.p",
                 type.one.p.co = "II.quart",
                 n.gen.conv = 150,
                 plots="no",
                 verbose="yes")
fitness_scores <- FitScore(res_GA)
GARS_PlotFitnessEvolution(fitness_scores)
Allfeat_names <- rownames(datanorm)
Allpopulations <- AllPop(res_GA)
GARS_PlotFeaturesUsage(Allpopulations,
                       Allfeat_names,
                       nFeat = 10)
data_reduced_GARS <- MatrixFeatures(res_GA)

workflows.name: find_optimal_features_loop
workflows.intent: Run GARS_GA across a range of chromosome lengths to identify the feature subset size that yields the highest fitness score.
input: datanorm (normalized SummarizedExperiment, matrix, or data.frame of expression data)
workflows.stages: 1. Loop through different chromosome lengths (chr.len) and run GARS_GA for each ;; 2. Extract the maximum fitness score for each run ;; 3. Identify the best population with the highest fitness score ;; 4. Extract the selected features from the best population
workflows.code:
populs <- list()
k=1
for (ik in c(7,8,9)){
  set.seed(1)
  cat(ik, "features","\n")
  populs[[k]] <- GARS_GA(data=datanorm,
                        classes = colData(datanorm),
                        chr.num = 100,
                        chr.len = ik,
                        generat = 20,
                        co.rate = 0.8,
                        mut.rate = 0.1,
                        n.elit = 10,
                        type.sel = "RW",
                        type.co = "one.p",
                        type.one.p.co = "II.quart",
                        n.gen.conv = 150,
                        plots = "no",
                        verbose="no")

  k <- k +1

}
max_fit <- 0

for (i in seq_len(length(populs))){
  max_fit[i] <- max(FitScore(populs[[i]]))
}
max_fit

best_popul <- populs[[which(max_fit == max(max_fit))]]
dim(MatrixFeatures(best_popul))[2]
